transcript:
Meeting: Aurora Edge — Redwood adapter strategy demo
Date: 2026-12-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (CTO, Aurora Edge), Elena Park (Lead ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Lina Gomez (Product)

Summary: Demo/walkthrough focused on mapping existing OpenAI/Anthropic/Together calls to Redwood API, adapter patterns, and pilot steps. Quick console tour and discussion of Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private.

Resources referenced: parity-sheet: https://drive.redwood.example/aurora-parity (placeholder), adapter-sample: https://github.com/redwood-inference/adapter-examples (placeholder), security-pack: https://redwood.app/security/soc2

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Marcus: Hey, good — thanks. We've been looking at consolidating vendors, so, um, eager to see how this maps.
00:12 Priya: Great. Quick agenda: parity mapping, adapter options, console quick tour, and proposed pilot. Feel free to interrupt.
01:02 Elena: Quick thing — our primary constraints are latency under 300ms p50 for short prompts, and cost target less than current per-token spend. Also we need function-calls parity for our toolchain.
01:20 Samir: Security is big too: SOC 2, SSO with SAML, customer-managed KMS if possible.
01:32 Jordan: Totally. We'll cover SSO/KMS in the security section — short answer: supported on Private and Dedicated with KMS integrations; hosted supports encryption at rest and audit logs.
02:00 Priya: Starting with the parity table — high level, there are three adapter patterns we usually recommend: 1) thin request-mapper that rewrites OpenAI/Anthropic API params to Redwood API, 2) sidecar adapter that handles streaming + function-call translation, 3) full SDK swap where you replace client calls with Redwood SDK and keep prompt templates.
02:30 Marcus: Hmm, can you give an example for function-calls? We use Anthropic-style tool calling for a retrieval pipeline.
03:00 Priya: Sure — Anthropic's tool call shapes are different, but Redwood supports structured function/tool calling. The adapter preserves the schema mapping: you map Anthropic's tool spec to Redwood's function definition and route the tool output back into your pipeline. There may be small differences in response keys, e.g., "tool_result" vs "output" — easy mapping.
03:40 Marcus: Are there any gotchas for streaming? Our UX depends on sub-second token streaming for chat.
04:05 Priya: Streaming is fully supported on Redwood hosted API — we stream tokens via SSE or websockets depending on client. In Dedicated/Private we recommend enabling continuous-batching thresholds carefully; if you do big batches you might increase latency. For sub-second live UX, reduce batch windows and use prefix caching.
05:00 Elena: Prefix caching?
05:12 Priya: Yeah, KV/prefix cache keeps repeated context in GPU memory so you don't re-tokenize or re-run prefix segments. It helps reduce p99 for repeated prompts, but it uses memory, so we balance with quantization and model size.
06:00 Samir: That sounds like KV cache — do we need special infra?
06:10 Priya: No special infra beyond what Redwood runtime manages. For Private, the cache is within the deployment; for Dedicated it's in our managed pool. It does require consistent session routing though, which we can do with sticky routing policies.
07:00 Jordan: Back on adapter patterns — for Aurora's case (you have OpenAI + Together traffic), I'd recommend starting with the thin request-mapper, run a 48-hour smoke benchmark, and then iterate to sidecar if you need to preserve streaming shapes or advanced function-call semantics.
07:35 Marcus: Ok. What about model parity? We're using OpenAI gpt-4-like endpoints and Together models for smaller tasks.
08:00 Priya: We maintain a model catalog with verified performance profiles. Parity mapping is two parts: 1) model capability mapping — pick Redwood-backed open models that match completion style and safety; 2) sampling/temperature mapping — e.g., Redwood sampling defaults might differ, so we expose the same top_p/temperature/penalty params. We'll share a spreadsheet mapping your current exact endpoints to recommended Redwood model variants.
09:00 Elena: How accurate is that mapping? We rely on very consistent behavior for system prompts.
09:15 Priya: It's not one-to-one always. For critical flows we recommend running the same prompts through both endpoints and capturing metrics: response length, token distribution, safety flags, and human eval. We can tie regression alerts into Redwood Optimize so you get notified if quality shifts.
10:00 Marcus: Great. Can you demo the console for setting routing and canarying?
10:20 Priya: Yep — quick share. (screen shares) This is the Redwood Console route config — you can set up multiple variants, percent rollouts, automatic fallback to cheaper model variants, and end-to-end tracing. For your canary, you can do 5% traffic to Redwood + 95% to existing vendor and compare latencies/costs.
11:05 Elena: Is tracing linked to user IDs? We need per-token tracing for debugging.
11:15 Priya: We have token-level traces and you can scrub PII via redaction rules. For Private deployments you keep full trace data; for hosted it's retained per your org retention settings.
12:00 Samir: About networking — our security team wants VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for encryption keys. How does that work?
12:20 Jordan: For Private, you run the control plane in your VPC (or we support a customer-managed control plane) and we integrate with your KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and a dedicated GPU pool; keys can be stored in your KMS with envelope encryption. We'll send the security pack and architecture diagram.
13:10 Marcus: What about compliance docs? Any SOC 2 or ISO certs?
13:20 Jordan: We have SOC 2 Type II and are working toward ISO 27001 — the security pack link is in the resources. We'll attach the certs in the follow-up.
14:00 Elena: Cost question — you mentioned batching reduces per-token cost. Is there guidance for chat use cases with many short prompts?
14:18 Priya: Short prompts are challenging; batching helps when you can tolerate slight added latency. Our Optimize engine suggests batching time windows and quantization profiles; e.g., for short chat you might prefer smaller batches + 4-bit quantization on the model to reduce GPU memory and cost while maintaining latency. We'll surface suggested configs based on your sample workload.
15:00 Marcus: Any vendor lock-in risks with adapter approach?
15:12 Priya: Minimal. A thin adapter is fairly portable — it's basically a translation layer. If you adopt deep SDK integration (SDK swap), you'll need some refactor but you'll also gain observability and performance improvements.
16:00 Jordan: Demo time — quick adapter example. Priya, can you walk the sample code?
16:06 Priya: Sure. (shares code) Here's a NodeJS request-mapper that accepts OpenAI payloads and emits Redwood requests. Note subtle differences: OpenAI 'messages' -> Redwood 'chat.inputs', and function-calls schema mapping. Also we handle streaming responses by polyfilling events.
17:00 Elena: I'm seeing a rename of response fields, that might break our parsers.
17:12 Priya: Right, so we include a compatibility shim in the adapter that maps keys back to the old shape. That shim is tiny and keeps your downstream the same.
18:00 Marcus: How long to get a pilot running? Ideally start next week.
18:08 Jordan: We can: timeline typically is 1) share adapter samples + parity sheet (48 hours), 2) customer runs smoke test with short traffic (48 hours), 3) pilot launch — a 1-week pilot either on Dedicated or Private depending on infra. So yes, next week is feasible.
19:00 Samir: Who owns the benchmarking? Redwood runs a managed benchmark or we run in our environment?
19:12 Priya: We can do both: Redwood SEs will run a benchmark in our environment for initial perf curves, but the real validation should run against your dev cluster to capture your network/hot cache patterns. We'll support test harness and scripts.
20:00 Elena: On the subject of model tuning, do you support finetuning or instruction-tuning on top of open models?
20:25 Priya: We support fine-tuning for select models and recommend retrieval-augmented generation via embeddings + reranking for most use cases. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization/tuning combos.
21:00 Jordan: Quick note on SLOs — Dedicated offers SLA-backed latency targets and reserved capacity. Hosted has SLAs but shared pools. Private is fully customer-managed. Pricing differences will be in the SOW.
22:00 Marcus: Any migration pitfalls you've seen?
22:15 Priya: Yeah — common ones: 1) mis-matched sampling leading to hallucination deltas, 2) streaming shape differences breaking UI, 3) overlooked rate limits on adapter endpoints. We include test suites and a sanity-check prompt set to catch regressions early.
23:00 Elena: Can you show how function-call differences get tested?
23:10 Priya: We automate function-call tests: you replay calls through both endpoints, validate schema and execution path, and compare outputs with a threshold for acceptable diffs. If diffs exceed thresholds, we flag for manual review.
24:00 (short silence)
24:20 Marcus: About Together — they have different tokenization subtly. Does that affect prompt length accounting?
24:40 Priya: Yes. Tokenization differences can change effective prompt length. We support token counters per model and will surface expected token counts. Adapter can also pre-normalize inputs to match tokenization where feasible.
25:30 Jordan: Let's talk telemetry: what traces do you need from Redwood for debugging?
25:40 Elena: Per request latency, token counts, model variant, and any safety flags.
26:00 Priya: We expose those in Console — you can filter traces by user, route, model. Also, we export metrics to Prometheus and logs to your SIEM for Private deployments.
27:00 Samir: For pilot, we need network diagrams and peering steps.
27:12 Jordan: We'll include a step-by-step peering guide and sample Terraform for peering/VPC in the follow-up.
28:00 Marcus: Ok, pricing ballpark?
28:10 Jordan: For pilot, token charges minimal; main costs are Dedicated reserved capacity if you choose that. I'll send a pilot estimate with two options: hosted + adapter vs Dedicated 2-week reserved pool.
29:00 Elena: Any references from existing customers?
29:10 Jordan: Sure, we'll include a short list— customers in fintech and health that did similar migrations.
30:00 (audible typing)
30:40 Priya: Quick console example of rollout config: set variant A (Redwood model v1) at 10%, variant B (fallback cheaper quantized) at 90%, and set automatic fallback on error codes. You can also configure per-route rate limits.
31:30 Elena: Good. Do you provide prebuilt adapter templates for Together and Anthropic?
31:40 Priya: Yes, we have starter adapters for OpenAI, Anthropic, Together in the repo I linked. They include polyfills for streaming and function-calls.
32:30 Marcus: On security again — audit logs retention? We need 12 months.
32:40 Jordan: Audit logs retention configurable per plan; Private supports extended retention on-prem, Dedicated we can do >=12 months with an add-on.
33:20 Samir: Does Redwood support customer-managed rotation of keys?
33:30 Jordan: Yes, we support KMS rotation and HSM-backed keys for Private. We'll document the exact flows.
34:00 Elena: Anything else on tooling?
34:10 Priya: Redwood Optimize also recommends quantization/model combos and can generate a cost/latency frontier so you can pick a config.
35:00 Marcus: Ok, let's capture clear next steps.
35:10 Jordan: Actions: Priya will send parity spreadsheet and adapter samples; Marcus will share sample traffic and top-10 prompt set; Samir will confirm VPC/KMS; Jordan will draft SOW.
36:00 (multiple agree)
36:30 Elena: One last thing — our legal team will want to see data-processing addendum and subprocessor list.
36:40 Jordan: We'll attach DPA and subprocessor doc in follow-up.
37:00 Marcus: Great, I'm optimistic. We want to start the smoke tests asap.
37:15 Jordan: Perfect. We'll aim to have the parity sheet and samples to you within 48 hours.
37:30 (wrap-up)
37:40 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and schedule the benchmark kickoff.
58:00 End of recording
